en: *The Supplementary Record of the Profound Meaning of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Scroll One, with Preface, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming during the Song Dynasty.
Question: Formerly, Dharma Master Baoyun once compiled a commentary on the *Profound Discernment* (*Xuánbiàn*), which was recently...
Master Gushan of the year [in question] further clarified the subtle purport through his commentaries and records; why then have I now compiled this work again?
I reply:
During Baoyun’s lecture series, disciples recorded the teachings as they went along, yet the meanings were occasionally incomplete and had not yet been revised when he unfortunately passed away.
The works produced by Gushan consist largely of textual exegesis and, moreover, eliminate the contemplation of the mind within their midst.

This is truly unbearable; therefore, I now take up my pen to recover the remaining meanings left by the former masters and to retrieve the texts discarded by later generations, so that the two paths of teaching and practice shall not fall into obstruction.
I address this only to those among the new students who have attained understanding; do not reproach me for my prolixity.
This preface was written on the full moon day of the fourth month in the first year of the Tiānshèng era, the year of Kǒihài.
The title consists of six characters: the first four refer to that which is explained (*vyākhyeya*), and the latter two refer to that which explains (*vyākhyāna*).

The latter is "universal" (*sāmānya*) because the Master of the Wise (*Bhadanta Vimuktisena*) established five meanings when explaining all sūtras; therefore, the former is used to distinguish this work from other sections.
The four characters of the sūtra title are explained extensively below in the text, and thus are not preface here.

Regarding the two characters "neng" (capable) and "shi" (to explain): "xuan" (profound) means that which is subtle and difficult to perceive; "yi" (meaning/principle) means that the underlying rationale is deep and possesses its own cause.

The profound and subtle meaning herein consists of five layers: namely, the names that express the beginning and end of this sutra, the essence they designate, the principle inherent in that essence, and the power and function by which that principle is realized; these four constitute the characteristics of the verbal teachings regarding their general and specific applications.

The Great Master investigated and extracted these five meanings to explain this single title, desiring that students first understand the essential purport of the sutra before examining its text, so that wisdom and practice may be established at every point of the text.

This is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where the cause of upholding [the Dharma] arises from stillness; it accords with the Buddha-mind and expounds this profound principle. Therefore, those who rely on obscure realization and those who merely seek the literal text cannot be spoken of as being on the same level.
How could such profound subtlety be a mere empty name?

One who can explain the Master’s title understands that "Tiantai" refers to the place where he dwelt in truth, "Zhizhe" is the title bestowed by the Sui Emperor, and "Great Master" (Dashi) is the model for all living beings. To "explain" here means to distinguish him from other masters and to take up the pen to compose his writings.
If the deeds from beginning to end were fully manifested in the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography), they are now omitted and not recorded here.

Second, the commentary on the text, which has two parts: first, the commentary on the preface; second, [the commentary on the main body]. First, the commentary on the preface, which has two parts: [1] ... [2] ...
First, a general indication of the essence of the Dharma.
"This" is a term used for specific designation.
"Suvarṇaprabhāsa" (Golden Light) is the essence of the Dharma being indicated.
"Profound and immeasurable" refers to the virtue of the essence of illumination.
One should know that these three characters in the distinct title of this sutra denote the Dharma itself and are not metaphors.
How is this known to be so?

The sutra describes the Tathāgata as roaming within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*—the sphere of action of all Buddhas—and while abiding in this samādhi, he proclaims: "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the king of all sūtras. Is this not a direct indication that the *dharmatā* in which he roams is itself named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, rather than stating that the *dharmatā* is like *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*?

As for the single interpretation of the analogies established in the subsequent text, it appears that various masters explain the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as worldly objects and phenomena, employing them as metaphors for the profound Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.

Although these various masters employ analogies to illustrate the Dharma, they do not in fact understand the perfect fusion of the characteristics of dharmas; they provide localized interpretations according to specific names, and for this reason, they are unable to use analogies to encompass all dharmas.

The Great Master, wishing to demonstrate that the ocean of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* contains no dharma that is not complete and no dharma that is not harmoniously integrated, follows the various masters by using the three characters of "Suvarṇaprabhāsa" as metaphors. These fully illustrate the sphere in which the Buddha dwells: briefly, they comprise the ten sets of three dharmas; extensively, they encompass all dharma-gates. Each and every one is mutually integrated, and all are inconceivable.
This is because the previous method of using external analogies was incomplete; therefore, I shall extensively reveal here how the nature of reality (dharmatā) is perfectly complete.

Although I have followed the approach of others by using analogies to illustrate the Dharma, the title of this sutra indicates that it is the Dharma itself and not a mere analogy. Consequently, I shall establish two types of interpretation—those based on the accompanying text and those based on the essential substance—to refute their reliance on inferential analogies which are remote from the truth. Only by relying on the sutra and adhering to the Dharma can one achieve true intimacy with its meaning.

This is because the Great Master profoundly understood the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): its venerable and precious nature is, in its essence, called "Gold"; its quiescence while constantly illuminating is, in its essence, called "Light"; and its great compassion that benefits all beings is, in its essence, termed "Clarity."
Thus, one knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is endowed with the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which is the ultimate accomplishment of the true meaning of its name.
Apart from the nature of phenomena, all names and expressions lack any real referent.

Therefore, regarding the three dharma-gates of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, taking one is to take all three, and the entirety of the three is one; they are neither three nor one, yet they are both one and three. Neither vertical nor horizontal, they transcend thought and discourse—this is the secret treasury where the Buddhas dwell.

Furthermore, it should be understood that that which reveals the essence of the Dharma through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* consists of five chapters as its essence. This is because this sutra takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its name, takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its essence, takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its central tenet, takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its function, and takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its pedagogical form.
Alternatively, the three characters may be correlated individually with the five chapters: taking "gold" as the essence, "light" as the principle, and "clarity" as the function;
taken collectively, these three constitute the name, while the differentiation of these three names constitutes the characteristics of the teaching.

Since the essence of the Dharma is thus, its attributes are likewise so. "Profound" is the attribute of light, for it exhausts the depths of the dharma-nature; "immeasurable" is the attribute of brilliance, for it reaches the limits of the dharma-nature. That these two are non-dual is the attribute of gold, for it signifies the ultimate nobility of the dharma-nature.
Furthermore, these three meanings are all profoundly deep, all immeasurable, and all non-dual.
The virtues of the five chapters are none other than thus.
Second, a specific clarification of the intent of the teaching.
Having already presented the general framework of the five chapters, we now specifically clarify the intent behind the establishment of this teaching.
First is the narrative on the intent of expounding the sutra, which refers to the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the five chapters;
second is the narrative on the intent of propagating and disseminating it, which refers to the Venerable Zhiyi’s circulation of the five chapters.
The first part itself consists of two sections:
First, the transcendence of words based on principle, because the ultimate truth can only be wondrously realized and is difficult to name accordingly;
second, the possibility of speech in accordance with conditions.
This is based on great compassion, which speaks without speaking; such speech necessarily benefits others.
The first section is further divided into two parts:
first, the analysis from the perspective of the self, wherein it is shown that from the highest fruit up to the most ordinary person, none can cause the sublime principle to be expressible in words.
This is further divided into three parts.
First, it is shown that no analogy can fully express the fruit of Buddhahood.
The four Buddhas spoke in verse: the weight of mountains, the drops of the ocean, the dust of the earth, and the realm of space—none of these can compare to the lifespan of the Śākyamuni Buddha.
Among these four metaphors, space is the greatest, for the three others—the mountains and so forth—depend upon space to exist.

Although space is vast, it is still an object manifested by the deluded mind; it arises through ignorance of the truth and ceases when one realizes its nature. Since it stands in opposition to the eyes and is accessible to the mind’s perception, how could it possibly serve as a complete metaphor for the inconceivable *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. How could one compare a single bubble to the great ocean?
Emptiness cannot be illustrated by anything; how could the three [realms] be discussed?
Question:

The sutra states that "emptiness and the like cannot be compared to the lifespan attained by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. Why, then, can it now be said that [the present case] is not comparable to the Great Awakened One or the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*?
Answer:

If the nature of awakening lacked even one of the three qualities such as gold, it would not be called "great. The meaning of the World-Honored One’s lifespan corresponds to clarity; if he did not possess the golden light, he would not have attained eternal life.

One dharma is not few, and three dharmas are not many; the arising of Buddhas and sentient beings is without difference, and essence and function are non-dual. If it were otherwise, it would not be the meaning of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings.
Even the metaphors of the four World-Honored Buddhas cannot reach it, demonstrating that the principle transcends words.
2. Clarifying that those at the stage of the cause have not yet exhausted the source.
Above, it was shown that although the Buddha as the fruition has reached ultimate realization, the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent; thus, even metaphors cannot manifest it.
Now, we examine that those at the stage of the cause have not yet reached the source of nature; therefore, even deliberation and conjecture do not suffice.
This consists of two parts:
first, a refutation by means of an analogy regarding wisdom and abandonment.

The blazing brilliance of the solar disc is a metaphor for the wisdom-virtue of *prajñā*; the eyes of an infant are a metaphor for the contemplative wisdom of emptiness and the provisional. Since these contradict fundamental wisdom, they are not the Buddha-eye; therefore, one cannot gaze upon them as one would the brilliant sun of wisdom-virtue.

The metaphor of the great ship with its watchtowers represents the liberation of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); the newly delivered woman represents the compassion based on conditions for arising phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*). Since this differs from the objectless compassion (*anālambana*), it lacks sublime power; therefore, it cannot be maintained upon the watchtowers of the virtue of abandonment.
This is based on the three wisdoms and three liberations of the perfect fruit, which serves to critique the compassion and wisdom of the bodhisattvas of the three preceding teachings.
If the cultivation of a perfect bodhisattva is identical to their inherent nature, then they are able, from the very beginning, not to deviate from these two virtues.

Nevertheless, although they are identical in principle, when viewed from the perspective of cause and fruit, there are differences in the clarity of wisdom and the strength of its power. For this reason, regarding the fruit, the wisdom and abandonment of the person [on the path] cannot yet be said to be "beholding" or "upholding"; one must understand that wisdom and abandonment are what is termed "light."
The non-duality of the two virtues is itself the Dharma-body, which is further named "Gold.
Although the two [terms] are used to exclude one another, this reveals that the source of the three dharmas has not yet been fully exhausted.
Second, the determination is made by means of the dharmas according to cause and effect.
Both the partial and the perfect bodhisattvas are able to subdue and sever [afflictions], and according to their respective practices, all are termed "pure.
However, because the dharma-nature practiced at the stage of the ultimate fruit of the Perfect Teaching transcends everything else, it is said to "surpass" them.
Even those who have attained ultimate realization through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* cannot adequately describe it; how much less can those who have not fathomed its source?
Third, clarifying why ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle are entirely deluded, in two parts:
first, the Lesser Vehicle.

Even Bodhisattvas of the partial and perfect vehicles, having aroused the vast and great mind and possessing the wisdom of partial realization, are still unable to fully express the principles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* through words that soar like elephants; how much less so can those of the two vehicles, who extinguish their minds to save themselves alone, be like the deaf looking toward the mute—how could they possibly conceive or speak of the sphere of action of the Buddhas?
2. The Ordinary Beings.

Although the worthies and sages of the Three Vehicles differ slightly from the Great [Vehicle]—in that their causes do not yet equal their fruits—they are nonetheless able to cultivate and realize the principle and wisdom of the three truths; yet they still cannot even conceive of or describe the ocean of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

How much more so for those of the common world and non-Buddhist paths, who are by nature outside this [teaching]; because they give rise to views based on words, their speech harms the reality, and since they cling to the absence of words, their silence leads to failure.
If one were to discuss speech exhaustively, there would be single words, compound phrases, and complete sentences;

if one were to discuss silence exhaustively, then beyond each of the three groups of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), there is one further instance of non-speech. Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīya school’s assertion of a "self" within the fifth category of the "inexpressible basket" (avaktavya-kośa) all represent the views on speech and silence held by heterodox outsiders.

Whether it be the indolent or those who study Buddhism, their minds focused solely on principle—whether speaking or remaining silent—in these two states increase their views and prolong their errors; though not identical to the *puruṣa* (divine self), they are entirely equivalent to the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*).

Therefore, the four teachings and four gates all give rise to views based on words; yet, departing from these four, one immediately gives rise to a view of wordlessness. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that the attachments of the five types of people all arise from grasping at the Tathāgatagarbha.
The one currently being rejected is precisely this person; therefore, it is said that both speech and silence are equally inadmissible.

Thus, having fully discussed the speech and silence of ordinary beings who give rise to views, the thought and discourse of the Two Vehicles who possess partial realization, and the wisdom and eloquence of Bodhisattvas whose realization is not yet ultimate—all these are incapable of expressing the nature of perfect completeness.

That even the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood—pure in mind and speech—cannot fully describe or realize it through explanation, serves to reveal that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is fundamentally secret: it transcends the characteristics of verbal expression and the characteristics of mental objects, causing the practitioner to relinquish words and forget conceptual deliberation.
II. Citation of Scriptural Evidence, in two parts:
first, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
That sūtra and its commentary clarify that although the brahmin Śreṇika was originally a heterodox outsider, his faculties were already mature; he approached the Buddha and requested: [text follows]
"May I obtain the eye of wisdom while remaining seated here without rising.
The Buddha opened his understanding for him, and he realized the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The Buddha then questioned him regarding the wisdom by which he had realized this principle:
“Is this wisdom attained through internal contemplation? He replied, “No.”
“Is this wisdom attained through observing the external, or the internal, or both together? They all replied: “No.”
"This refers to the four phrases where both speech and conceptualization are utterly extinguished; only then does one attain the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
If even those of small wisdom are thus, how much more so the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*?
Second, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*."
The first passage generally subsumes all discourse on thought; furthermore, the subsequent "birth of birth" (sheng-sheng) and so forth specifically forget the fourfold discourse.

Our school uses this to subsume the path of speech and thought within the four teachings: that which is truly produced by causes and conditions, and because it is the dharma produced, is called the "birth of birth," namely the Tripitaka Teaching.
That the arising of illusory existence is itself non-arising is called "arising that is non-arising"; this is the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
That one abides not in non-arising yet establishes the arising of the ten realms is called "non-arising arising"; this is the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

Regarding why the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is called "non-arising of non-arising": in principle, there is fundamentally no arising; since phenomena are identical to principle, phenomena likewise do not arise. Thus, it is termed "non-arising of non-arising."
The nature is fundamentally unarisen; practicing in accordance with this nature is itself the nature, and practice, too, is unarisen—thus, these two are both unarisen.
Because the substance of delusion is empty, it does not arise; because the function of wisdom is forgotten, it does not arise—thus, these two are both unarisen.
Because there is no cause that can be cultivated, it does not arise; because there is no fruit that can be attained, it does not arise; thus, both do not arise.
Since the nature of all relative phenomena—such as self and other, response and stimulus—is fundamentally non-dual and primordially quiescent, the term "non-arising" is stated twice for emphasis.
Regarding the statement that all four types are "inexpressible," there are two intended meanings:
first, from the perspective of their respective domains, the principles of the four teachings can only be realized through wisdom and are entirely inexpressible.
Śāriputra said: "Within liberation there is no verbal expression; this is the Tripiṭaka.
The three [disciples] likewise use the path of wordlessness to sever all afflictions; this is the Abhidharma."
The Silent Boy does not speak because he is neither ordinary nor holy, neither existent nor empty; this refers to differentiation (*bhedana*).
All phenomena are quiescent and cannot be expressed in words; this refers to perfection (*pariniṣpanna*).

If one transcends these stages, the perfectly wondrous principle cannot be demonstrated by means of the four modes of discourse; it is difficult even to describe it fully, let alone through the three teachings.
Thus, all of this reveals that the *Golden Light* Dharma is a secret treasury, inconceivable.
Second, it can be explained according to conditions.

Although the principle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is free from marks and quiescent, if one realizes it by transcending conceptual thought, then through the four *siddhāntas*, one may speak where there is nothing to say, thereby enabling sentient beings to obtain immeasurable benefit.
The text itself is divided into four parts.
First, it clarifies that there must be an occasion for speaking.

Following the four kinds of the "Ineffable" (*anirvacanīya*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it states: "Because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken. Is this not precisely the case of making fourfold explanations in accordance with conditions?
Regarding the statement that there are causes and conditions, these refer to the ten links of dependent origination.
Among the twelve links, only the two branches of future birth and death are excluded, as these are the results produced by those causes and conditions.
From past ignorance to present existence—these ten are all productive causes and conditions that can bring about the fruits obtained through the four teachings.
Why is this so?

Since the link of ignorance is precisely the mind of craving and grasping from the past, and because this mind exists, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest the various names and meanings of the four teachings.
Having both craved and grasped, one then gives rise to the four types of karmic action based on the Four Teachings; this is "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*).

This karma is able to sustain the consciousness of the person who has received the teachings as it enters the mother's womb; this is "volitional formations condition consciousness" (*saṃskāra-pratyaya-vijñāna*).

This consciousness, following the karmic conditions of the four teachings, forms the fourfold fruits such as name-and-form; that is to say, consciousness conditions name-and-form, up to contact conditioning feeling.

Since the four types of teachings have already induced the five fruits in this present life, one consequently craves those same four teachings within the mind that experiences them; this is "conditioned by feeling, there is craving.
One inevitably seeks out and grasps the dharmas of the four teachings; this is "conditioned by craving, there is grasping."
If craving and grasping are profound, one can diligently cultivate the four types of teachings to bring about existence; this is precisely "grasping conditions existence.
Since existence inevitably brings forth its fruit, one will thereby achieve the fruits of the noble ones in the present and future.

Because sentient beings possess ten causes and conditions, the noble ones have taught the four methods of instruction: to cause those who have not yet planted [the seeds] to plant them, to cause those who have already planted them to ripen, and to cause those who have already ripened to attain liberation. It is said that these bring about such benefits; therefore, one must not fail to teach in accordance with these conditions.
II. Clarifying that this teaching is worthy of veneration.

Generally speaking, in accordance with conditions, there are the four teachings throughout a single lifetime; now, specifically addressing the capacities of sentient beings, the five meanings of this sutra are revealed.
Each of these five meanings is individually most venerable, and they are further divided into two parts:
First, the five meanings of the sūtra are enumerated.
Regarding "named after gold" and so forth: the name consists of three characters, and at least two of these must necessarily be present.
Because gold is supreme, its radiance is likewise so.

Taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its essence, although it pervades all things, the sphere where the Tathāgata dwells is restricted solely to the realization of the fruit; this is the height of pervasiveness and the ultimate of restriction.
As for the specific meaning of the title, that which is indicated by these three characters is precisely the ultimate primary truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "adorned bodhisattvas" and so forth: in the subsequent text, the established thesis specifically takes the fruit as its focus.
Here, the term "bodhisattva" refers to one who has realized the fruit.
Since they are able to adorn profound and wondrous merits, this represents the ultimate profundity and wonder of the four virtues of the fruit.
Although the words contain the cause, the intent lies precisely in the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "illuminating all the heavens" and so forth: the various devas and spirits are all great bodhisattvas; when the light of the *dharmatā* shines upon them, their progress on the Path will surely increase. Therefore, the great provisional beings give rise to Dharma-joy, manifesting the power and function of the Sūtra as both vast and profound.

Regarding the phrase "the title 'King of Sutras' and so forth," this section contains many passages that describe the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as the king among all sutras; because a king is able to exercise sovereign command, its teaching subsumes all other scriptures.
However, this commentary explains the King of Sutras by unifying its principles and expressions as the Middle Way.
Furthermore, this sutra is itself a king, for it attains mastery over the nine types of sutras.

The words are that which express, and the principle is that which is expressed; because the words and the principle are unified, the subject and object mutually merge. Whether it be the teaching or the principle, both are called the Middle Way, and all are the King of Sutras.
In the *Śāstra*, the essence of the King of Sutras is described, which refers to the Middle Way as that which is explained;
now, in the King of Sutras, the teaching itself is described, which refers to the Middle Way as that which explains.
If it were not for the Middle Way teaching,
there would be no way to explain the principle of the Middle Way.
Be careful not to provide biased interpretations by using the names of other schools to claim they represent the Middle Way teaching.
Second, the conclusion indicating its venerability:

It is noble because it is named after gold; it is ultimate because it takes the principle of the fruit as its essence; its doctrine is profound because it is the finality of the three bodies; and its function is great because there is nothing it does not benefit.
The letters themselves are the Middle Way; therefore, the teaching is called the King. For this reason, each of the five chapters is lofty and expansive.
Third, because it clarifies the Honored One, all sages protect and uphold it, in two parts:
first, protection and upholding by the ultimate fruit.

That which is expressed—the wondrous middle wherein all phenomena converge—is named the non-dual essence. Because all Tathāgatas have realized this essence, they rely upon it to abide and maintain it, constantly guarding and mindful of it so that the eight inversions do not arise in sentient beings.

Because the sutra expresses four types of wisdom, it mentions four Buddhas; however, in reality, this essence is not one that any Buddha does not protect. Therefore, it says that "the three periods and the ten directions are likewise so," and as the subsequent sutra states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sutra in mind."
2. Veneration by those of Great Expedient Power.

Regarding "all bodhisattvas and others," the *Praise of the Buddha* chapter below states: "At that time, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas departed from this world for the land of the Tathāgata Golden Jewel Canopy Mountain King."
Having arrived in that land, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Buddha; with palms joined toward the Buddha, they praised him in unison.
The Commentary states: "The assembly of those offering praise is set forth as having reached that land"; therefore, it is said that they pay remote homage by pervading all other directions.
Regarding the passage "the tree deity, the virtuous daughter, and others," this is also from the text of this chapter.
In the verses of praise by the Bodhi-tree deity, it says: "I have constantly practiced the supreme great compassion; weeping and shedding tears of sorrow, I long to behold the Buddha."

Regarding the phrase "the various devas cover [them]," this is explained extensively in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," the "Chapter on Vajrapāṇi" (Saṃjñeya), and the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits. They constantly use their supernormal powers to protect those who preach and listen, as well as the kings and their respective territories.

The "Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā," the "Chapter on Mahāpratisarā," and the "Chapter on Śrī-devī" each extensively explain within their respective sections those who practice the path of benefiting others.

These bodhisattvas and celestial deities are for the most part former Buddhas who have returned, or perhaps partial manifestations of the Truth descending in response; they pay distant homage and extol the merits of the Tathāgata, protecting and benefiting both those who preach and those who listen. This is all done out of devotion to the King of Sutras and the desire to circulate the Vaipulya teachings; were it not for the supreme subtlety of this Dharma-gate, how could they provide such diligent assistance?
Fourth, because it is clearly expounded, its benefits are comprehensive and vast.

Regarding "all that exists is completely dried up," the "Chapter on Repentance" states: "Within the three realms of existence, the great ocean of birth and death surges with turbulent waves that agitate and disturb my mind; its flavor is bitter and poisonous, most coarse and harsh. The Net-Luminosity Tathāgata can cause it to dry up and vanish."
This is because there are none who do not transcend the three realms of existence—desire, form, and formlessness.

Regarding the phrase "removing the heat and affliction of the three miserable paths," the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" states: "This sutra can cause the rivers of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts to burn up, dry out, and become parched."

Regarding the summary and so forth, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" states: "At that time, all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, through the Buddha's spiritual power, experienced celestial bliss; those with incomplete sense faculties immediately attained their full restoration."
To state the essentials: all unprecedented matters of benefit throughout every world appear in their entirety.

The benefits of expounding this sutra do not merely consist in removing the retributive sufferings of the three miserable realms; one must clarify how the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) are freed from suffering in ten stages and attain happiness in ten stages, thereby enabling the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* to manifest in its ultimate form—only then can it be said that the characteristics of the appearance of these unprecedented matters have been fully discussed.
II. Exposition of the Intent of the Proclamation.
What has been clarified above—how the principle of primordial quiescence accords with conditions to establish the teaching—all describes the intent of the Tathāgata in preaching the sūtras.

Now, this wise person personally describes his own intellectual power to grasp the meaning and explain the title; this is the intention of clarifying the meaning based on the text to penetrate the sūtra.
This section is divided into four parts:
first, the noble one’s praise of the protector.

When one wishes to engage in discourse, one should first reflect upon how the supreme sages praised [the Dharma] incessantly and protected it without weariness; thus, the aspiration to emulate the sages has its own long-standing origin.

Regarding the "Praise by King Sāgara" (Jīnlóng sānshì zàntàn) over three lifetimes: the Bodhisattva Xìnxiàng was a king in the past named King Sāgara (Jīnlóngzūn), who extensively expounded verses and praises for all Buddhas, vowing to encounter Śākyamuni Buddha in the future.
Now, having fulfilled his aspiration, he shall praise the Buddha with verses within this assembly.
The Honored King Golden Dragon praised him in the past, and the Bodhisattva Faith-Aspect praises him in the present.

Furthermore, there is a vow that for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the future, in every place of birth, one shall see a golden drum in dreams at night and speak of it according to reality during the day; this is the praise of the future.
This refers to the praise of that single body throughout the three periods of time.
Question:
Since the Golden Dragon praises the Buddha throughout the three periods of time, how can it be said to proclaim the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* in their stead?
Since the person and the dharma are distinct, how can they be harmonized? Answer:

By taking up the unsurpassed, true dharma of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, one constitutes the unsurpassed, provisional person of the fruit-Buddha. Apart from the dharma there is no person; apart from the person there is no dharma. The words praising the Buddha are precisely the proclamation of the subtle mind and form; this mind and form is itself the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

Just as the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa took refuge in the Triple Gem—regarding the Great Compassionate Savior as the Buddha, his physical marks and characteristics as the Dharma, and praising the Buddha was, in essence, extolling the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*.
Regarding the Earth Deities and others, their chapter on firm resolve states that they said to the Buddha:
"Wherever this sutra is circulated, we shall prepare a lion throne and cause the Dharma-preacher to sit upon it to proclaim this sutra extensively."
"I shall always serve as his attendant therein, concealing my form beneath the Dharma-seat and supporting his feet upon my head.
It is because the supreme sages revere the Dharma that they honor the person.
2. Regarding the general rules for teachers:

If even the two sages, who had attained profound realization, praised [the Dharma] throughout kalpas and humbled themselves to venerate and protect it, how much more so should those of the lower stage of ordinary beings, who receive the teachings and strive in their practice, not propagate them widely?
Third, relying on the meaning to give rise to words:
relying on the principle of the aforementioned sages who protected the Dharma, I give rise to the words of these five chapters that penetrate the sutra.
Fourth, praising the Dharma to seek benefit.
The dew and birds serve as metaphors for the goodness of one who masters the sutras;
entering the sea and heading toward the mountains serves as a metaphor for this goodness conforming to one's nature.
Truly, it relies upon a slight condition, which is precisely the aforementioned goodness.
To have one's color become uniformly salty is precisely the benefit we now hope for.
This means that even a tiny drop of slight goodness is wished to share the single salty flavor of the ocean of nature.
May even a fragmentary condition of a bird or beast share the single wondrous color of the Buddha-mountain.

The mountain is called Sumeru, composed of four precious substances: gold in the east, silver in the west, lapis lazuli in the south, and crystal in the north; birds dwelling near each side take on the color corresponding to that location.
Nevertheless, even a single thought of sympathetic joy has merit equal to empty space; how could the circulation of the Five Grades [of Practice] have a virtue comparable to a mere drop of dew?

It was specifically because the Great Master looked upon ordinary beings from the perspective of the sages, humbled himself while honoring the sutra, and intended to admonish future generations not to be self-conceited or boastful.
2. Explanation of the Profound Meaning (Xuanyi), in two parts:
first, listing the chapters and providing the structural outline.
First, the explanation of the title, which constitutes the Profound Meaning itself;
Second is the explanation of the text, which refers to the actual words and phrases.

Since the title of this fascicle is simply given as "Profound Meaning" (Xuanyi), the structural outline follows this convention; therefore, the two topical headings of "Explanation of the Title" and "Explanation of the Text" are not listed.

Now, in presenting this outline and structural analysis (*pian*), what prevents us from interpreting it as an explanation of the subsequent textual passages? We shall instead judge that the current *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) serves as an explanation of the title.
Within this explanation of the title, five chapters are first listed; these are the subjects to be explained.
Regarding these five chapters, two types of explanation are provided, namely the general and the specific, as both of these explanations interpret all five chapters.
Second, the explanation according to the topical outline has two parts: first, the general explanation, which has two [subdivisions]: [The rest of the text follows.]
First, the arising;
second, the differentiation.
If one were to provide a comprehensive general explanation, it would be like the *Fahua xuanyi*, which provides a general explanation of the five chapters in seven sections:
First, the presentation of the heading, so that it may be easily remembered and upheld, thereby giving rise to a mindful mind;
second, the citation of evidence, based on the Buddha’s words, so as to give rise to a mind of faith;
third, the generation [of the practice], so that the mind may arise without distraction and enter into meditative concentration.
Fourth, opening and closing;
fifth, distinguishing and examining;
sixth, reconciling differences, for the purpose of giving rise to the mind of wisdom.
Seventh is the contemplation of the mind, which means that upon hearing [the teaching], one immediately cultivates it by giving rise to a mind of diligent effort.
The present text abbreviates this, providing only two sections.
It involves the arising of only two minds:

The arising [of concentration] gives rise to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and the discernment [of wisdom] gives rise to insight (*prajñā*). If concentration and insight are established, all practices are accomplished.
Of these two, the first is "arising.
It is called "initial" because it is that which designates [the subsequent].
Names are provisional and must necessarily rely upon real dharmas, namely sound.
It is through the modulation of sound that names and phrases are formed.
Since one traces the provisional back to the real, this treatise discusses the Buddha’s work of transformation through vocal sounds in this land.
However, if one follows the Buddha or a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the name is derived from sound.

If one follows a scriptural volume, although the name is derived from form, that form—the original scripture—is a compilation of the teaching of sounds; therefore, following the scriptural volume is also called "hearing the name."
This follows the initial reception of names and phrases from one's own practice.
As for "the essence being second," the name is the signifier, like a finger pointing at the moon;
the essence is the signified, like the moon pointed out by that finger.
If one loses the meaning, they grasp at the finger as being the moon; not only are they deluded regarding the moon, but they have also lost the finger.
If one grasps the meaning, they forget the name to attain the essence; not only do they recognize the essence, but they are also not oblivious to the name.
Now, this treatise aims at attaining the ultimate meaning; therefore, having moved beyond the stage of merely hearing the name, one next recognizes the essence of the Dharma.

That the "Principle" (zong) occupies the third position is because the Principle is itself practice (*caryā*); practice is that which can advance toward the goal, leading from cause to fruit. If one does not recognize the essence, then practice cannot be accomplished.
This explanation remains generally applicable.

If the first three teachings involve realizing the Middle Truth of reality, cultivating contemplation by taking that truth as an object, they may also be termed "practices for the sequential manifestation of the essence.
Now, we clarify that in the Perfect Teaching, cultivation arises entirely from nature; if one does not recognize nature, what could serve as cultivation?

Nature is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), while cultivation is initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). Original enlightenment is free from thought and pervades all places; it is precisely by means of this awakening that one constitutes initial enlightenment.
Therefore, the inconceivable realm is itself contemplation; only this practice of contemplation constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zong*).
Thus, one should know that while the substance is manifest and the sequence of the text is broad, the meaning is concise; this must be well understood.
As for the fourfold function, it exists because the thesis is established, whereby it possesses effective power.
To say that "the thesis is established" means that the essence has been fully revealed.
The entire essence gives rise to the thesis, and the thesis in turn reveals the essence; the entire mirror emits light, and the light in turn reveals the mirror.
Once the mirror has been polished until it is perfectly clear, no image will fail to appear;
thus, when the fundamental principle is established, it can universally benefit all things.
As for the teaching that follows, it is through its application that it is able to benefit all things.
The method for benefiting sentient beings lies in the administration of instruction; thus, there are five types of instruction.

Regarding those that "hear the name" and so forth: both names and instructions are capable of explicating principle (*yukti*). However, based on the distinction between self-benefit and benefit-for-others, two chapters are divided:

the chapter titled according to "names" concerns the initial reception of practice for one's own cultivation, while the chapter titled according to "instructions" concerns the initial application of teaching for the transformation of others.
Regarding "having a beginning and having an end," this refers to the two aspects of beginning and end.
Seeking the name to attain the essence and establishing the fundamental principle to give rise to its function constitutes the beginning and end of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).
Bestowing teachings to benefit others, such that they likewise seek the name and even give rise to its function, likewise constitutes the beginning and end [of benefiting others].
Thus we know that the five chapters have two beginnings and two endings;
the text cites the two beginnings, while their two endings emerge from the context.
Second, the section on "Discrimination" has two parts:
First, the preliminary investigation has three parts:
first, the posing of the question.
This establishes the inquiry by means of the most concise and the most extensive [explanations], thereby introducing the response given from the intermediate standpoint.
2. Answering the Objections.
If the names and enumerations are too numerous and extensive, those who practice contemplation will find them difficult to memorize and will retreat, discouraged by their vastness.
If the chapters and sections are too brief and general, they will fail to fully clarify the meaning, and those who study the teachings will be unable to develop understanding.

Therefore, five chapters are established, with their length and brevity attaining the middle way; thus, practitioners shall achieve both the realization of meaning and contemplative observation, making it easy to clearly understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Third, the conclusion and demonstration.
2. Analysis, in two parts:
first, the actual analysis, in two parts;
first, [the analysis] in terms of six types.

This refers to the six pairs—general and specific, principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, teaching and practice, self and other, and speaking and silence—which constitute the discernment of the five chapters.
Regarding "general and specific," the preceding chapter constitutes the explanation of names (*nāman*).
The three characters "Jin," "Guang," and "Ming" collectively constitute the designating names (*nāman*).
As for the subsequent triad, they correspond respectively to the essence (*tattva*), the thesis (*siddhānta*), and the function (*kārya*).

To distinguish these three characters individually: "Jin" (Gold) specifically corresponds to the essence; "Guang" (Light) specifically corresponds to the thesis; and "Ming" (Radiance) specifically corresponds to the function; therefore, they are termed "distinct."
The final chapter concerns the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsanalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the inclusion of both the general and the specific: this refers to the characteristics of the flavors of the teachings within the four chapters, distinguished as general and specific.
Next, regarding principle and phenomena (*tattva* and *dharma*): the essence is the principle revealed by the four chapters, while the four chapters are the phenomena arising from that essence.

Regarding the three [sets of] cause and effect, where the first three are causes and the latter two are effects, this is based on the clarification of the fundamental tenet (*mūla*) below, which establishes them definitively as effects.
It should properly state, "The first two are causes and the latter three are effects"; I suspect the text contains an error.
However, the essence itself is neither cause nor effect; rather, it is the principle manifested by cause and effect.

To seek the essence through its name is still like manifesting the principle through faith and understanding within the "cause" [member of the syllogism]; it is not yet the principle manifested when the thesis is established as the result, and therefore it is categorized as belonging to the cause.
Regarding the four teachings and practices: the first four are "practices" because they are taught in contrast to what follows; therefore, the former are all practices. Why is this?
Names are the phenomena of practice, substance is the root of practice, the principle is the fruit of practice, and function is the virtue of practice.

Regarding the five [categories] of self and others, all five chapters are again designated as "practice" (*caryā*); yet, the first four are divided and categorized as practices for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*).
As for that which pertains to one's own benefit, because it is applied with mastery and its conditions and causes are manifest, it still belongs to the category of one's own benefit.
Only the final section on establishing the teachings belongs to benefiting others;
all these are termed "practice" because both forms of benefit are being enacted therein.
Regarding the sixth, "speech and silence": since the four preceding chapters pertain to one's own practice, they all require the forgetting of words, and thus they all belong to silence.
The latter one transforms others by responding to their capacities and establishing teachings; therefore, it is what should be explained.
Both are called "sages" because being free from speech and silence is the dharma of a sage.
2. Applying this principle to other meanings.

Beyond these six categories, various other meanings—such as understanding and practice, cultivation and realization, bondage and liberation, essence and function, and response and resonance—all can be analyzed according to the characteristics of the five chapters; however, for fear of prolixity, they have been omitted here.
2. Manifestation by means of analogies, in two parts:
first, establishing the analogy.
"Manifest" (xian) here means to demonstrate (shi).
"Appropriately central" refers to the five chapters.
"Clearly manifesting and encompassing abundance" refers to the virtues of both the Dharma and its metaphors.
Encompassing abundance is like having jewels within a bag; being clearly manifest is like reaching in to show them to others.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Explaining the Buddha’s sūtras is like having a treasure within a bag; if the opening is tied shut, people will not know of it. One should untie the bag of the Buddha’s sūtras and explain its underlying principles."
Now it is the same here: by means of this single analogy, six pairs are revealed; therefore, it is said that "all are provided as analogies for analysis.
Second, the six types are correlated.
The general resides within the particular, and the particular resides within the general; this can be seen through analogies.
In principle, there are four chapters, like a bag containing treasures.
The entirety of the principle establishes these four, like reaching in to show them to others.
Because the fruit’s virtues are complete within the cause, it is like a bag containing treasure.
Because the fruit is manifested from the cause, it is like reaching in to show it to others.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) regarding the teaching is like a bag containing treasure.
The teachings clarify practice, just as pointing out the way to someone.
One must personally cultivate the methods for benefiting others, just as one who possesses jewels in their bag.
Then, by means of that personal cultivation, one benefits others, just as pointing out the way to someone.
Silent and perfect realization is like a treasure within a bag;
explaining according to that realization is like reaching in to show it to others.
Not only these six pairs, but all things may be illustrated by such analogies.
2. Specific Explanation.
The preceding section was a general explanation because each individual item was treated in relation to all five chapters; hence it was called a "general explanation.

Now, however, the five chapters are explained one by one. When explaining a name, the other four are not mentioned, and this is likewise the case when explaining the other four; therefore, this constitutes a "specific explanation."
The main section is divided into five parts.
First, the explanation of the title.
"Title" refers here to the names and terms listed throughout this treatise; for the sake of providing a general overview, the formal heading is taken as the title.
This consists of two parts, namely the general and the specific names.
The single character "Sūtra" (經) is the general name, as it applies universally to all sections [of the canon].
The three characters "Jin" (金) and so forth are the specific name, as they specifically title this particular sūtra.

Now, when our school explains the titles of various sutras, we simply divide them into the two categories of the general and the specific; we do not state that the "sutra" is the signifier while the remainder is the signified.
Those who receive the teachings of our mountain school must take care to understand this.
First, the explanation of the specific title has two parts.
First, it is established that there is no contradiction between the detailed and abbreviated versions of the three or five titles.

This is because the present four-fascicle version is a translation by Dharmakṣema; it designates the specific title as merely the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light) and lacks the two characters "di-wang" (Emperor-King).
If one examines the title of the seven-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha, the characters "Emperor and King" (帝王) appear following "Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
Although these words "Emperor and King" do not appear in the title of this [present] edition, the sense of being the "King of Sūtras" is present within the text itself.
Therefore, regarding the explanation of the title, there is no contradiction in either explaining or not explaining those two characters.

Furthermore, as the Great Master frequently proclaimed this scripture, the inclusion or omission of the Emperor’s name at the time of explaining the title was appropriate to the occasion; thus, the profound text inherently possesses both extensive and abbreviated versions.
Second, the explanation according to the sequence of the text and its meaning, in two parts:
first, the initial explanation of the three characters based on the text, in two sub-sections;
first, the explanation according to the meaning of the teaching, which means that the teaching elucidates the underlying principles.
Second, the explanation by way of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the cultivation of practice through meditation.

This serves to clarify both the teachings and the practices of our school, as well as to present both the meaning and the contemplation together, so that those who receive these instructions may achieve success in their understanding and practice.
Regarding the first two [sections]:
first, the heading and enumeration.
Among the five [categories], the first two include both general and specific titles, while the latter three consist solely of specific names.
Among the three [categories], the first follows ancient conventions while the latter two represent only the present meaning.
Within the second [category], there are both phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*) as they appear in the text, whereas the third refers solely to the principle in its essential nature.
II. The Correct Explanation, in five parts:
A. The General and the Particular, in two parts:
1. Distinguishing and Indicating the General and the Particular, in four parts:
First, a general clarification of the threefold distinction between the universal (*tong*) and the particular (*bie*).

This is because the Great Master’s profound understanding of these two names does not merely refer to the universal and particular teachings; it likewise refers to the universal and particular practices as well as the universal and particular principles. Thus, it is said that based on the teachings one clarifies practice—wherein practice possesses both the universal and the particular—and from practice one manifests principle—wherein principle possesses both the universal and the particular. Therefore, the threefold distinction between the universal and the particular is all invoked by these two names.

Therefore, among the various schools, there are those that establish these two names based solely on principle; for instance, in the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and others, "garbha" (matrix/store) refers specifically to the principle of the wondrous conventional, while "sūtra" (discourse) refers to the principle in its universal sense.

There are those who establish two names based solely on their practice: namely, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Samādhi-sūtra*. Since the *Śūraṅgama* differs from the samādhis of the partial and small vehicles, it is a distinct practice (*bie xing*), whereas the sūtra itself is a universal practice (*tong xing*).

There are those who establish two names based solely on the teachings themselves: namely, the *Śāriputra-parivarta Sūtra* (Yijiao jing) and others. Since the *Yijiao* differs from the various other teachings, it constitutes the Separate Teaching (biejiao), while the "sūtra" itself constitutes the Universal Teaching (tongjiao).
Alternatively, "teaching" (*śāsana*) may be taken as the specific name and "the principle of practice" (*pratipatti-yukti*) as the general name, as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts.
Since "speaking" is the teaching, the sūtras spoken therein constitute the principle of practice.
Alternatively, one may take "principle" as the specific name and "teaching" as the general name, as in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* and other such texts.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is like a jewel, and this sūtra is like a casket; thus, the teaching contains the principle.
Moreover, among the various schools, there are not few that take principle as their scripture.
Yet this school claims, "The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sutra in mind.

The *Avataṃsaka* says, "By breaking a single atom, one brings forth a great scroll of the sutra. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says, "This treasury of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is profound, firm, remote, and deep; no one can reach it," and further states, "Being protected and remembered by all Buddhas, planting the roots of myriad virtues, entering the stage of right determination, and giving rise to the mind to save all sentient beings—by accomplishing these four dharmas, one obtains this sutra."

The Commentary states: "The four phrases are precisely the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). Since this knowledge and vision constitutes the sutra, is it not the wondrous principle?

To take practice as the sutra is as stated in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*: "All Buddhas extend their broad and long tongues and speak words of truth. You sentient beings should believe this sutra which praises inconceivable merit and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas."
Since you have pointed out that the merit is what is protected by the sutra, does it not follow that the sutra itself is not a practice?
The Buddha then raises a question himself:
"What is called 'the sutra protected and kept in mind by all Buddhas'?"

The Buddha himself explained: "If sons or daughters of good family hear this sutra and accept and uphold it, as well as hear the names of the various Buddhas, these people shall be protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and they will attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
Using the sūtras one upholds and contemplates as the question and taking the practitioner who is able to cultivate them as the answer—is this not to treat practice itself as the sūtra?

Furthermore, in the *Great Amitābha Sūtra*, when that Buddha discusses practice, he always refers to it as "expounding the sūtra. Thus, we know that there are many instances where the principle of practice is designated as the sūtra; one cannot restrict the term "sūtra" solely to the name of the teaching.
The "Comprehensive" (tong) aspect already possesses the three elements of teaching, practice, and principle; the distinct names for possessing these three are clearly evident.
Second, distinguishing the two uses of the teaching.

Third, the comprehensive and the distinct across the three [aspects]. Since our school’s explanations of the titles of the various sections have already been detailed, we shall set those two aside and instead clarify the characteristics of the comprehensive and the distinct specifically with respect to the teaching.
This single interpretation alone is already capable of distinguishing it from the interpretations of other schools regarding the title.

Why is this? It is because those masters take the character *jīng* (sūtra) alone to be the teaching that expresses (*neng-quán*), while they regard the remaining characters as the principle expressed (*suǒ-quán*); how could they know that both names reside within the teaching itself?
Third, clarifying the function of the teachings.
The universal and particular teachings are established in mutual dependence, for they are able to express the underlying principles.
Question:

This statement—that principle is without names and that names are called "principle"—seems to be in immediate contradiction with the section on the "Essential Nature" which asserts that the True Truth has names while the Conventional Truth is nameless. How are these two views to be harmonized?
Answer:
That [text] distinguishes between the ultimate and the conventional; this [text] clarifies principle and teaching.
That [text] takes that which is expounded by the Perfect Teaching as the ultimate, while taking what is perceived by ordinary people as the conventional.
Since the ultimate meaning and name are inherently present in the absolute (zhen), it is said to have a name;
since the conventional (su) lacks substantial meaning, it is said to be nameless.

Now, both principle and teaching are discussed here according to the Perfect Teaching (yuan). That principle is without names and words serves to manifest original quiescence and to transcend the marks of names and words.

Regarding "names name the principle": this does not refer to the names of ordinary people that cling to appearances; rather, it refers to the names of the Perfect Teaching that accord with reality. Because the principle possesses inherent virtues capable of responding to all names, there is not a single name that does not name the principle.

Take the analogy of space, which has neither length nor shortness, yet can correspond to the measurements of length and shortness; therefore, every single *zhang* and every single *chi* is nothing other than space.

The "Chapter on Realizing the Essence" states that since the existence of names in the ultimate truth is discussed from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching, it is not an existence of fixed existence, but rather the name of the nameless.

Therefore, the "existence of names" therein and the "namelessness" here are identical in meaning; they correspond to what the *Awakening of Faith* says regarding the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which first clarifies its transcendence of language and subsequently clarifies its reliance upon language—though these two meanings are distinguished, they are in fact one True Suchness.
Therefore, Jingxi said:
"Nature is fundamentally nameless, yet it fully possesses all names.
Thus, one knows that the present text and the "Chapter on the Essential Substance" are virtually without discrepancy.
Furthermore, it cites the meaning of *dhāraṇī* from the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*: although there are no words, it is called "retention" (*dhāraṇī*).
If one does not fully possess the true names and meanings, how could it be termed "retention"?
Fourth, the correct elucidation of the commonality and particularity of the teaching.
Although the functional efficacy of the teaching has already been discussed above, its common and particular essences have not yet been explicitly clarified.
Now, taking words and letters as the general essence of the teaching refers to the means by which it teaches as its distinct essence.
Why is this so? Whether elucidating good or elucidating evil, or demonstrating the partial or demonstrating the perfect, all employ words and letters; thus, the teaching is universal.
The reason for this is that it can express the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*).
Written characters revolve according to that intent; because the intents differ, the teachings become distinct.
One should understand that what is entirely pervasive constitutes the distinction, since written characters are employed to express the reasons [for those teachings].
The particular and the universal are not separate, for they employ words according to their intended meaning.
Since both the universal and the particular now reside within the teaching, both are capable of revealing [the truth].
II. The General and Specific Aspects of the Sutra Title, in two parts:
A. Universally demonstrating all sections, in two parts: 1.
Directly employing the general and specific aspects to explain the title, in two parts: [subsequent sub-points].
First, the general [explanation].

The Holy One’s teachings encompass the entire body of scriptural instruction; there is nothing that is not comprised within these written words. When [the scriptures] speak of "one" from the beginning to the end of their discourse, they are simply citing one instance as a representative example.

To take a single sutra from among the many scriptures, or even a single word from among the various sayings: in terms of arrangement, they range from the broad to the narrow; in terms of number, there are few at the beginning and many at the end—meaning that while sutras may be few, their time [of teaching] is many, and so on, up to sentences being few while words are many. All such instances are the teachings of the Sage. Since every teaching necessarily consists of written characters, we know that written characters constitute the universal essence of the teaching.
Because they penetrate through the written words, they are collectively termed "sūtras.
Second, the specific [classification], which has two parts:
first, clarifying the specific characteristics, which refers to the reasons by which [the sūtras] can manifest [the truth].
Although the intentions behind the words and phrases spoken by the Sage are manifold, their meaning is fully encompassed within the four *siddhāntas* without exception.

The *loka-siddhānta* ensures that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) remains undisturbed; for instance, the *Avataṃsaka* differs from the *Āgamas*, and the *Vaipulya* differs from the *Prajñāpāramitā*, all in order to inspire joy.
The *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals) varies according to what is appropriate, so as to cause them to give rise to wholesome states.
The *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remediation) differs according to the specific conditions for destroying evil, so as to cause the extinction of transgressions.
The first is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth), which, by differentiating the capacities of those who enter into principle, brings about wondrous awakening;
for this reason, it is said that the names and characteristics of the various sutras differ.
Second, the summary of the four *siddhāntas*.
Joy and suitability correspond to awakening; these may be understood by pairing them with the four [benefits].
If one explains that all sutras arise from the four *siddhāntas*, since the four here and the four there differ in meaning, for this reason the various sutras are designated as distinct.
Second, the metaphors illustrating the general and specific aspects that constitute the teaching:

salt and plum represent the combination of the warp and woof of the salty and the sour, which serve as metaphors for the general and specific functions of the written words; likewise, flavor and embroidery serve as metaphors for the differences between the names and characteristics of the various sutras.
Second, the definitive judgment regarding this sutra has two parts:
first, explaining it according to its specific [classification].
Regarding the phrase "The reason why," etc., this specifically clarifies the fourfold *siddhārtha* (purposes) of the present sutra.
There are those with the capacity for the world who, upon hearing of the three bodies, joyfully praise their eternal function.
There are those with the capacity for persons who, upon hearing praises of the three bodies, give rise to wholesome roots.
There are those with the capacity for remediation who are able to cultivate repentance to destroy the evils of the three obstructions.
There are those with the capacity for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), who are destined to awaken to the principle of the sphere of action of all Buddhas.
It is with this distinct intention that this sutra was preached.

Although there are four [levels of] audiences (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*), all derive benefit from the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*; therefore, the three characters [of the title] are set forth to manifest the distinction of this teaching.

Regarding the phrase "from the commonality of language and so forth": although the four *siddhāntas* differ across various sūtras, each one necessarily requires written characters (*vyañjana*). Since the substance of written characters pervades all sections [of the canon], the word "sūtra" is used here to indicate that the teaching is universal.

Although the current title follows the *Chen* (Paramārtha) version, the title of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* translated by Paramārtha is the most detailed; therefore, the Master employed it to establish the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit titles.

These four qualities exist inherently as the Dharma-body; when the nature fully gives rise to cultivation, the three wisdoms are necessarily perfected. When wisdom merges with the inherent virtues of the nature, the nature itself possesses these four qualities.
From the perspective of illuminating the ultimate meaning, it is called only *prajñā* (wisdom), for when wisdom accords with the nature, liberation responds to the capacity of beings.

Since it arises entirely from the nature, it necessarily constitutes the three liberations; therefore, the same nature possesses the four virtues, yet from the perspective of the arising of its function, it is called only "liberation" (*vimukti*).

Regarding the abandonment of the immeasurable and the adoption of these ten types: it is because these ten encompass both the adverse and the favorable, and include everything from beginning to end, such that both sequences form a systematic progression.
II. The Correct Arising, in two parts:
First, tracing back from the teaching of the Dharma to show that principle is revealed through phenomena;
second, practicing the path in its forward progression to return to the True from the delusory.

Regarding the arising of these two: first, from the non-abiding foundation of the dharma-nature, all teachings are established; second, from the non-abiding foundation of ignorance, all conditioned phenomena are established.
Question:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without abiding, yet it is established within the teachings; upon what textual authority is this stated?
Answer:

This passage belongs to the "Section on the Essential Substance," which clarifies that all sages establish their names based upon the Truth; it thus cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."

Since this proof has already been cited to show that names are established based on the True [Dharmatā], is it not the case that all teachings are established precisely because the Dharma-nature is non-abiding?
Nevertheless, if one were to discuss in full detail how all phenomena are established from the root of non-abiding, they would not exceed four levels.
As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"In principle, there are the inherent qualities of the conditions and the understanding; in phenomena, there are the cultivated qualities of the three causes. In delusion, one flows through the three paths; in awakening, these become the supreme functions within the fruit."
These four layers are all established based on the delusion regarding the true reality (dharmatā); the former [passage] refers to that text.

Now, the first section here corresponds to the superior function within the fourth fruit of that text, while the latter section here corresponds to the three causes of cultivated virtue within its second [section].
Question:

In the first section on arising, from the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*) down to the three paths, these should collectively correspond to delusion and thus involve the circulation through the three paths;
why, then, are the teachings established here in contrast to the superior functions within the fruition?
Answer:

Now, regarding what is called the "Secret Treasury," it is clearly manifested through the Three Jewels and so forth. How could one be deluded about the principle and yet rely upon the Three Jewels and the various triads of dharmas?
Therefore, it should be understood that an interpretation based on the principle that the teaching arises from the principle is alone appropriate.

Moreover, the present arising of the two types—contrary and conformable—is identical in intent to the arising of the four meanings of stage, wisdom, gate, and contemplation as explained in the *Fahua Wenshu* (The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) regarding the sequence of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering."

Therefore, that *Wenju* states: "The vision of principle arises from the stages; the establishment of the stages arises from wisdom; the activation of wisdom arises from the gates; and the opening of the gates arises from contemplation.

Because of contemplation, the gates open; because the gates open, wisdom is perfected; because wisdom is perfected, the stages are established; and because the stages are established, one sees the principle."

The *Commentary* explains: "Regarding this sequential and reverse arising, the first part clarifies the 'object' (the dependent) by means of the 'subject' (the dependent-on), and the second part clarifies the 'subject' (the dependent-on) as manifesting the 'object' (the dependent).
Is it not the case that in the first section of the present text, the 'object' is clarified by means of the 'subject'?
Does not the former [the subject] then manifest the latter [the object]?
Having grasped this meaning, one may then interpret the text.
Regarding the first passage: the principle of the three virtues is the Buddha’s ultimate realization; transcending all names and characteristics, it is called the "Secret Treasury" (guhyagarbha).

The manifestation of this treasury results from the union of awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) and the principle of non-awakening; for this reason, the Tathāgata manifests the Three Jewels (*triratna*).
As these Three Jewels are established through the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), they are said to be the three types of nirvāṇa.
The attainment of nirvāṇa further depends upon wisdom and virtue; therefore, the three bodies (trikāya) are taught.
Since the bodies are reached by means of the vehicles, the three great vehicles (trimahāyāna) are taught.
Since the vehicles are traversed by means of practice, the three types of enlightenment (tribodhi) are taught.
Because Bodhi is illuminated by wisdom, the three types of Prajñā are taught.
Because Prajñā arises from nature, the three Buddha-natures are taught.
Because the seed-nature fundamentally originates from the understanding of names and meanings, the three consciousnesses are taught.
Since consciousness and understanding fundamentally arise from the three obstacles as their very principle, they are spoken of as the three paths.

All are entirely due to the secret nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and its lack of fixed abiding; therefore, the Great Sage takes this non-abiding nature of reality as the foundation to establish the nine names and characteristics, as well as all the teachings.
This present arising serves as the basis for the subsequent explanation of the ten dharmas.

To explain the following passage: above, it was demonstrated that the Great Enlightenment realizes the treasury of the three virtues; because it is non-abiding, it establishes all the teachings of the Dharma, culminating in the three paths.

Now, we shall distinguish how sentient beings abide within the three paths; because they do not dwell [in a fixed state], they bring about the phenomena of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and ultimately proceed toward the three virtues.

Furthermore, the three paths take ignorance (*avidyā*) as their beginning; because ignorance is manifest, karma and suffering both revolve. By transforming delusion into liberation, one comes to discern the sacred teachings, and thus the three consciousnesses are formed.
Understanding is the seed of the vehicle, which is precisely termed the cause of Buddhahood; thus, the three Buddha-natures are established.
Because the seeds permeate original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya), wisdom is aroused, and these are termed the three Prajñās.

The wisdom of the path of practice proceeds along the great straight path to achieve *sambodhi*. When the practice of wisdom accords with the nature of reality, there is nothing it does not sustain; thus it achieves the three Great Vehicles.
By discerning the wisdom of retribution through these vehicles, it is darkly attuned above and responds below, thereby achieving the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The body is eternally free from delusion, neither arising nor ceasing; this is called the threefold nirvāṇa.
Through mastery over the virtue of cessation, one bestows grace and benefits all beings, thereby manifesting the Three Jewels.
Once the merit of benefiting others is perfected, both self and others find rest, together returning to the three virtues.
This present arising establishes the basis for the ten successive stages of contemplating the mind that follow.
Third, the summary and demonstration:
by tracing back the origins of the teachings and following them in the practice of contemplative cultivation, all are brought into a systematic order.
2. Regarding the ten dharmas as all being lofty and vast by way of their immeasurable profundity, there are three parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the explanation, which has two sub-sections: [The text continues with the explanation.]
First, explaining the immeasurability by way of universal inclusion, in three parts:
first, explaining that each possesses ten dharmas.
Since the dharma-realm of the three virtues is boundless, what dharma-gate is there that it does not encompass?
Furthermore, its essentials are comprised of nine aspects.

Its intrinsic nature is fundamentally eternal, blissful, self, and pure; thus it is termed the "Three Virtues" (triguṇa). That which is capable of possessing these and that which is possessed constitute the ten dharmas.
Since this is the case for the three virtues, it can be understood by implication that the remaining nine are mutually complete; therefore, they are not presented in full detail.
Second, explaining that each possesses all:
since the "one possessing nine" was explained based on essential points, one should know that each and every one possesses all three dharma-gates.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unimpeded and capable of responding to all numerical categories; therefore, a single dharma-gate can encompass all dharma-gates of the number one, as well as all dharma-gates of the number two, and so on, up to and including every dharma-gate of names and numbers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that none cannot be contained within it.
